questions.title: Why does the Federal Circuit apply regional circuit law when reviewing a denial of JMOL in a patent case?
questions.question_body: In *Finesse Wireless v. AT&T*, the court explicitly states it reviews the district court's denial of JMOL under the law of the regional circuit (here, the Fifth Circuit), yet it reviews claim construction de novo under Federal Circuit law. I am confused about the jurisdictional split here. Since patent law is supposed to be national to promote uniformity, why does the standard for reviewing a procedural motion like JMOL depend on the regional circuit, while substantive patent issues do not? Does this create a risk of forum shopping based on the regional circuit's JMOL standards?

questions.title: When does contradictory expert testimony fail to support a jury's infringement finding under the substantial evidence standard?
questions.question_body: The court reversed the JMOL denial for the '134 patent because the plaintiff's expert testimony regarding the 'interference generating signals' was self-contradictory. The expert initially mapped the signals one way, then pivoted when cross-examined, but never clearly clarified the mapping. I understand that appellate courts review jury findings for 'substantial evidence,' but at what point does contradictory testimony render the evidence insufficient? Is there a specific test for when an expert's confusion or change of course negates the jury's ability to rely on that testimony?

questions.title: Does amending a claim from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals' constitute clear and unambiguous disavowal of scope?
questions.question_body: Regarding the '775 patent, the court analyzed whether Finesse surrendered claim scope over two signals when it amended the claims from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals' to overcome an obviousness rejection. The court held this did not rise to the level of 'clear and unambiguous disavowal.' I'm struggling with the prosecution history estoppel standard here. If an amendment is made specifically to distinguish prior art that used two signals, doesn't that imply an intent to surrender the two-signal scope? What distinguishes this from a situation where an amendment clearly disavows scope?

questions.title: How does the Federal Circuit distinguish between 'separately identifiable' and 'unique' signals in claim construction?
questions.question_body: The district court construed the limitation 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' as 'separately identifiable' but not 'unique,' relying partly on inventor testimony. The Federal Circuit agreed. I am confused about the semantic difference in this context. If the signals are 'separately identifiable,' doesn't that imply they are distinct entities? How can they be the same signal (non-unique) yet still be separately identifiable in the context of a mathematical multiplication limitation? How much weight does inventor testimony carry when it seems to contradict the plain language of listing three distinct variables?

questions.title: Can a patentee cure a lack of evidence mapping claim limitations to the accused device through post-hoc clarification on appeal?
questions.question_body: In the '775 patent analysis, the court noted that the expert did not testify at trial how the three distinct multiplications in the accused device mapped to the seven claimed multiplications. Finesse attempted to clarify this mapping in their appellate brief. The court rejected this, stating the evidence was never presented to the jury. I want to understand the boundary here: If the evidence exists in the record (e.g., in documents) but wasn't explicitly mapped by the expert at trial, is it ever permissible for the appellate court to consider that mapping to find substantial evidence, or must the mapping be explicitly made by the expert during the trial?

questions.title: Why did the Federal Circuit vacate the damages award rather than remand for a new damages trial after reversing the infringement finding?
questions.question_body: The court reversed the denial of JMOL of noninfringement for all asserted claims and subsequently vacated the damages award. I would have expected the court to remand for a new trial on damages, perhaps to see if there was infringement on non-asserted claims or if a different damages calculation was possible. Why is the procedural remedy simply vacatur when the underlying infringement finding is overturned? Does the vacatur imply that no damages are recoverable at all, or is it just clearing the slate for a potential retrial on infringement?
